patient.chief_complaint: Subtle cognitive decline over 6 weeks in well-compensated NASH cirrhosis patient
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. A. is a 58-year-old accountant with well-compensated NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, MELD 8), obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, and type 2 diabetes, presenting at his wife's insistence for cognitive evaluation. She noticed 6 weeks of progressive forgetfulness, difficulty with sequential tasks at work (he made errors in spreadsheets he normally manages perfectly), increased irritability, and a reversal of sleep pattern (day drowsiness, nighttime wakefulness). He denies confusion, but psychometric testing reveals mild impairment. He has no jaundice, no ascites, no asterixis. His ammonia is 48 µmol/L — at the upper limit of normal (lab ULN 45 µmol/L). His CT head is essentially normal. His EEG shows subtle slowing. On review, his SpO2 is 96% and his wife reports he frequently removes the CPAP mask overnight. He takes omeprazole and metformin.

output.proposed: OSA management optimization — CPAP non-compliance contributing to cognitive decline and worsening HE
interactions: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) with CPAP non-compliance: nocturnal hypoxemia worsens hepatic ammonia metabolism — hypoxia reduces urea cycle enzymatic activity in the liver
OSA independently causes cognitive impairment (attention, processing speed) — additive with HE
contraindications: Sedating sleep aids in CPAP non-compliant patient — risking further hypoxemia and HE worsening
warnings: CPAP compliance <4 h/night is considered non-compliant — insufficient to prevent hypoxemia
Nocturnal oxygen supplementation is NOT a substitute for CPAP — does not reverse obstructive events
alternatives: CPAP mask refit and patient education
Positional therapy adjunct (supine sleep worsens OSA)
Referral to sleep medicine for adherence optimization
AutoPAP device may improve compliance over fixed-pressure CPAP

output.proposed: Assess omeprazole 5-year use as HE precipitant in cirrhosis
interactions: PPIs alter gut microbiome (dysbiosis) — increase urease-producing bacteria → increased ammonia production; multiple studies show PPI use is associated with HE in cirrhosis
Omeprazole long-term use (5 years) in cirrhosis: increased risk of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) → more ammonia
contraindications: PPIs without clear ongoing indication should be reassessed in cirrhosis
warnings: PPI deprescription trial: switch to as-needed H2 blocker (famotidine) — reassess HE after 4 weeks without PPI
alternatives: Famotidine 20 mg PRN as PPI substitute
Reassess H. pylori status — treat if positive (reduces gastric ammonia production)
If GERD poorly controlled, consider brief re-introduction of PPI at lowest effective dose

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Covert/minimal hepatic encephalopathy (PHES -5), well-compensated NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, MELD 8) — precipitated by CPAP non-compliance (nocturnal hypoxemia impairs ammonia metabolism) and long-term PPI use (gut dysbiosis); ammonia borderline (48 µmol/L); no asterixis.

differential.diagnosis: Obstructive sleep apnea cognitive decline (untreated CPAP)
differential.key_features: Untreated OSA causes cognitive dysfunction; addressing CPAP adherence may resolve some symptoms.
PHES is sensitive to covert HE specifically; AD workup if PHES improves with HE management and symptoms persist.

optimal_actions.action: Comprehensive labs: CMP including AST/ALT/bilirubin/INR/albumin, ammonia, CBC, glucose, electrolytes (Na, K, Mg), BUN/Cr, lactate, blood cultures and urine cultures; toxicology if substance use plausible. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 48 (borderline); cirrhosis features (Child-Pugh A); TSH; B12; folate.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline non-contrast — exclude alternate structural cause of cognitive decline.

optimal_actions.action: Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (Covert/minimal HE; PHES testing; PPI and gut dysbiosis; OSA and HE).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering omeprazole (REASSESS necessity), metformin, CPAP adherence counseling, lactulose initiation; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: PHES psychometric battery — diagnostic gold standard for covert HE.
Consult hepatology + sleep medicine for CPAP optimization — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — consider if PHES improvement does not match clinical improvement. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
FDG PET has no role in HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy is reversible with precipitant control and does not require nuclear functional imaging.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: PHES testing to formally diagnose covert HE.
Trial lactulose 30 mL TID titrated to 2-3 soft stools/day; re-test PHES at 4-6 weeks.
CPAP adherence optimization with sleep medicine.
Reassess long-term PPI necessity; deprescribe if not indicated; consider H2 blocker if needed.
Driver-safety counseling — covert HE impairs driving (well-documented).
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not dismiss subtle cognitive complaints in a cirrhotic just because ammonia is 'low' or Child-Pugh is 'good'.
Avoid starting cholinesterase inhibitors before confirming HE is the diagnosis.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Covert/minimal HE affects ~30-50% of compensated cirrhotics; PHES is the diagnostic gold standard; treatment reduces overt HE risk and improves QOL (AASLD).
PPIs have been associated with HE risk via gut dysbiosis; deprescribe when not indicated.
Driving safety is impaired in covert HE — counsel and document.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss HE concern because liver disease is mild.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Covert HE occurs in compensated cirrhotics; PHES sensitivity does not depend on Child-Pugh class.
Ammonia correlates poorly with HE grade; covert HE is diagnosed psychometrically (PHES), not by ammonia.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: covert/minimal HE in well-compensated NASH cirrhosis (MELD 8); borderline ammonia 48; no asterixis; CPAP non-compliance and PPI use as non-obvious precipitants; PHES testing is the definitive diagnostic tool; patient appears well with subtle cognitive decline only
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Subtle presentation in well-compensated patient; PHES required; multiple subtle modifiable contributors (CPAP, PPI); easy miss in routine practice.
